title: Diego Garcia
description: Atoll in the Chagos Archipelago, Indian Ocean
wiki_lead:
Diego Garcia () is a coral atoll in the central Indian Ocean, the largest and southernmost of the atolls of the Chagos Archipelago. Its nearly continuous, V-shaped rim of land, about 64 kilometres (40 mi) long, almost encloses a lagoon of 124 square kilometres (48 sq mi) and holds more than half of the archipelago's land. Administered by the United Kingdom as part of the British Indian Ocean Territory (BIOT), and claimed by Mauritius, it is the site of a joint British–American military base, Naval Support Facility Diego Garcia; it has no permanent inhabitants, and around 2,000 military personnel, officials and contractors are ordinarily present.
Known to Portuguese navigators from the early 16th century and claimed by France from 1769, the atoll was settled from the 1780s by planters from Île de France (Mauritius) with enslaved workers brought mainly from Madagascar and Mozambique. It passed to Britain with Mauritius in 1810–1814, and for 150 years its plantations at East Point, Pointe Marianne and Minni Minni produced coconut oil and copra; it was briefly a coaling station in the 1880s and a flying-boat base in the Second World War. The descendants of the plantation workers formed a community known as the Ilois, now generally called Chagossians.
In 1965 the United Kingdom detached the archipelago from Mauritius to form the BIOT and, under the 1966 UK–US exchange of notes, made it available for the defence purposes of both governments. The inhabitants of Diego Garcia were removed in 1971, and the rest of the archipelago was emptied by 1973 (see Expulsion of the Chagossians). An American naval communications station built from 1971 was expanded under the Diego Garcia Agreement 1976 into a naval support facility, which has since been used for operations in the Gulf, Iraq and Afghanistan; in 2008 the British government acknowledged that the island had been used for two American extraordinary rendition flights in 2002.
The atoll is at the centre of the Chagos Archipelago sovereignty dispute: in 2019 the International Court of Justice advised that the United Kingdom should end its administration of the archipelago "as rapidly as possible". Under the treaty signed on 22 May 2025, the United Kingdom would accept that "Mauritius is sovereign over the Chagos Archipelago in its entirety, including Diego Garcia", and Mauritius would authorise it to exercise sovereign rights over Diego Garcia for an initial 99 years. After the position of the US president, Donald Trump, changed in 2026, the British government said that it could not ratify the treaty without American support, and as of November 2026 it had not entered into force. In March 2026, during the war between the United States, Israel and Iran, two Iranian ballistic missiles were launched towards the island; according to the British Defence Secretary, neither got close to it.

It passed to Britain with Mauritius in 1810–1814, and for 150 years its plantations at East Point, Pointe Marianne and Minni Minni produced coconut oil and copra; it was briefly a coaling station in the 1880s and a flying-boat base in the Second World War. An American naval communications station built from 1971 was expanded under the Diego Garcia Agreement 1976 into a naval support facility, which has since been used for operations in the Gulf, Iraq and Afghanistan; in 2008 the British government acknowledged that the island had been used for two American extraordinary rendition flights in 2002.
The atoll is at the centre of the Chagos Archipelago sovereignty dispute: in 2019 the International Court of Justice advised that the United Kingdom should end its administration of the archipelago "as rapidly as possible". Under the treaty signed on 22 May 2025, the United Kingdom would accept that "Mauritius is sovereign over the Chagos Archipelago in its entirety, including Diego Garcia", and Mauritius would authorise it to exercise sovereign rights over Diego Garcia for an initial 99 years. After the position of the US president, Donald Trump, changed in 2026, the British government said that it could not ratify the treaty without American support, and as of November 2026 it had not entered into force. In March 2026, during the war between the United States, Israel and Iran, two Iranian ballistic missiles were launched towards the island; according to the British Defence Secretary, neither got close to it.


Names

The origin of the name is uncertain. The former BIOT Commissioner Richard Edis mentioned a possible combination of the names of two Portuguese fleet commanders, Diego Lopes and Garcia de Noronha, and an account of a visit by a Spanish navigator named Diego Garcia in 1532, but regarded any explanation as speculation; early maps used other names, such as Don Garzia, and the present name became definitive only in the late 18th century. Mauritius's pleadings attribute the discovery of the archipelago to Diego García de Moguer. Edis thought that the Portuguese discoverer of the archipelago was probably Pedro Mascarenhas.
Visitors have compared the shape of the atoll to "a serpent bent double", in the words of the 19th-century Mauritian historian Charles Grant, and to a horseshoe, and its late-20th-century American residents to a footprint in the sand, with the islets at the mouth of the lagoon forming the toes. The United States Navy calls the island the "Footprint of Freedom". The people born in the archipelago came to call themselves Ilois, "islanders". Places on the atoll keep plantation-era names such as East Point, Pointe Marianne, Minni Minni and Barachois Sylvain, and at Cannon Point two six-inch guns have pointed out to sea since 1942. According to Edis, the names of Eclipse and Observatory Points, at the lagoon entrance, probably come from the observation of an eclipse of Jupiter's moons by the surveyor Archibald Blair in 1786.


Geography


Location
Diego Garcia lies in the south-east of the Chagos Archipelago, on the Chagos–Laccadive Ridge, a volcanic ridge that continues northwards through the Maldives and Lakshadweep. It is the southernmost of the archipelago's five atolls with islands, the others being Peros Banhos, the Salomon Islands, the Great Chagos Bank and the Egmont Islands. According to the United Kingdom, the atoll is 690 nautical miles (1,280 km) from Malé, 962 nautical miles from Agaléga, the nearest Mauritian territory, 970 from Colombo and 1,140 from Port Louis.


Atoll and islets
The atoll has a total area of about 170 square kilometres (66 sq mi), of which the lagoon occupies 124 square kilometres (48 sq mi) and the land about 30 square kilometres (12 sq mi). It has a dry-land rim that stretches about 64 kilometres (40 mi) from end to end, which the US Navy describes as "one of the most continuous land rims of any atoll in the world", broken only by a pass about 6 kilometres (4 mi) wide at the northern end. The rim varies from a few hundred metres to about 2.4 kilometres (1.5 mi) in width, being widest at the north-west, where the main settlement lies. The geographer David Stoddart, who studied it in 1967, described it as a typical mid-ocean atoll on a subsiding volcanic foundation.

Three islets lie in the lagoon entrance: West Island, Middle Island and East Island, the largest. A fourth, Anniversary Island, a sand cay at the north-western end of Spur Reef, was named in November 1990 for the territory's 25th anniversary. The seaward reef flats are generally 50–250 m wide and mostly remain slightly submerged even at low spring tides; beyond them the outer slope drops steeply, to more than 450 m within about a kilometre of the shore in places.


Lagoon

The lagoon is about 21 km long and up to 11 km wide. For an atoll of its size it is shallow, with a maximum depth of 31 m in the survey made by HMS Vidal in 1967, and it is divided into three basins. Knolls rise from its floor, but almost none of them reaches the surface outside the 10 m line, and Stoddart judged that Diego Garcia "must be almost unique among atolls in the absence of surface patch reefs in the lagoon". The lagoon opens to the sea only through three passes in the north, Main Pass, Middle Pass and Barton Pass, of which Main Pass, the westernmost, is the widest and deepest.
In the south the lagoon shore is deeply indented by barachois, inlets with narrow mouths that open into wide intertidal flats; the largest are Barachois Sylvain, about 2 km long, and Barachois Maurice, about 4 km long. The northern part of the lagoon has been altered by the dredging of an anchorage, a turning basin and an access channel 13.6 m deep for the military facility, and Hamylton and East estimated that about 0.55 km3 of sediment had been removed from the north-west of the lagoon between 1967 and 1998.


Elevation, soils and fresh water
Most of the land is only 1–1.5 m above sea level. The highest ground is on the ocean side, where coastal dunes have formed along about 17 km of shore; Stoddart levelled the dunes at Pointe Marianne at almost 7 m above low water, and the US Navy gives dune heights of 4.5–9 m. Much of the eastern arm is so narrow and low that it floods extensively at high spring tides. The sediments are almost entirely calcium carbonate, with fragments of pumice, and a dark-brown peaty loam a few inches deep has formed on the higher and older parts of the atoll.
In 1770 the French officer La Fontaine reported that the island was "not provided with fresh water", but beneath the wider parts of the rim lie lenses of fresh water that float on the denser seawater and are recharged by rain; shallow wells tap them readily. The base's water system has drawn on the lenses since 1978, about 90 per cent of its supply coming in 2005 from the well field near the cantonment, and in the late 1990s 102 wells in five production areas yielded about 1 million US gallons (3,800 m3) a day, the pumping rates being adjusted to keep the chloride content acceptable. The lenses are vulnerable to salt-water intrusion and pollution: use of the airfield well field was suspended after a fuel spill in 1991. A few freshwater marshes recharge the lenses, notably in the receiver antenna field in the north and near the Pointe Marianne cemetery, where the marsh is noted for its ferns, aquatic plants, fish and eels.


Coastal change
Comparing Stoddart's map of 1967 with satellite images of 2005, Hamylton and East found that 26 of 69 transects across the rim had eroded and 43 had accreted, much of the accretion being the building out of the lagoon shore for the airbase, which had added an estimated 3.01 km2 of land. Charles Sheppard disputed the findings, pointing to increasing inundation of the low south-east of the atoll and to the cost of hardening parts of the shoreline of the base. In 2025 the territory's Chief Scientific Adviser reported that Diego Garcia risked a breach of its southern narrows.


Climate

Diego Garcia has a hot, humid and very wet climate, with a mean temperature of about 27 °C in every month and relative humidity averaging about 79 per cent. The seasons are governed by the north–south migration of a zone of equatorial westerlies between the north-east and south-east trade winds: winds are variable but mainly westerly from December to March, April and May are a transition, the south-east trades blow steadily from June to September, and October and November form a second transition. Winds of more than 40 knots are unusual.
Mean annual rainfall was 2,599 mm in the records for 1937–38 and 1951–66, with annual totals ranging from 1,465 to 3,805 mm; rain is heaviest in January, February and October, and monthly falls average less than 200 mm only during the trades, from April to August. Because of the low latitude, tropical cyclones are rare; according to the Mauritius meteorological service, a cyclone of moderate strength passed just south of the atoll on 16–17 September 1944 and destroyed two Catalina flying boats. The US Navy notes that cyclones seldom pass close to Diego Garcia, because many form near it and then move away.


Oceanography and hazards
The archipelago lies at the eastern edge of the Seychelles–Chagos thermocline ridge, a year-round feature between 5° and 10°S where the thermocline comes close to the surface; it marks the boundary between the westward South Equatorial Current to the south and the eastward South Equatorial Countercurrent to the north. Tides are semi-diurnal; records made at East Point in 1967 gave a maximum range of 1.6 m at spring tides and 0.7 m at neaps. Analyses of the island's tide-gauge records, kept since 1988, have differed, one finding no statistically significant long-term rise to 2011 and another a rise of 6.22 mm a year between 2003 and 2015.
Earthquake shocks are felt at times, as the area lies on a minor plate margin. On 30 November 1983 an earthquake of magnitude 7.3 in the Chagos region damaged buildings and piers on Diego Garcia, ruptured underground fuel lines and caused a small tsunami that damaged the south-east of the island. The tsunami of 26 December 2004 registered 60 cm on the tide gauge at Diego Garcia; the US Navy reported no impact on its facilities and attributed this largely to the ocean topography, including the depth of the nearby Chagos Trench.

grok_lead: Diego Garcia is a V-shaped coral atoll and the largest island in the Chagos Archipelago, located in the central Indian Ocean at approximately 7Â°S latitude and 72Â°E longitude, forming the principal landmass of the British Indian Ocean Territory. The atoll, spanning about 44 square kilometers with a lagoon nearly 19 kilometers long, hosts Naval Support Facility Diego Garcia, a joint United KingdomâUnited States military installation established in the 1970s following the 1966 bilateral exchange of notes that authorized its development for strategic logistics and support roles. Its remote position enables prepositioning of materiel, aerial refueling, and sustainment for operations across the Indian Ocean region and beyond, serving as a critical node for U.S. Central, European, Africa, and Indo-Pacific combatant commands without direct exposure to littoral threats. The base's construction necessitated the closure of copra plantations and the compulsory relocation of roughly 1,500â2,000 Chagossian inhabitants from the Chagos islands to Mauritius and the Seychelles between 1968 and 1973, a process tied to securing the site for unrestricted military use. In 2024, the UK reached an agreement with Mauritius to transfer sovereignty over the Chagos Archipelago, including Diego Garcia, while preserving the base's operations through a 99-year leasing arrangement with the United States, though the deal has faced objections from U.S. President Donald Trump in January 2026, leading to reopened discussions and potential risks to its implementation. On March 20, 2026, Iran launched two ballistic missiles targeting the joint US-UK military base on Diego Garcia. The attack was unsuccessful: one missile failed mid-flight and a U.S. destroyer launched SM-3 interceptors at the second, though it could not be determined if an interception occurred; neither reached the target or caused damage, demonstrating Iran's extended missile range capabilities. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte stated the alliance could not confirm Israel's claim of Iranian involvement or intercontinental capabilities, but emphasized assessing Iran's missile threat and supporting US responses. Iran denied responsibility, with a senior official stating to Al Jazeera that Tehran was not behind the strikes. The UK foreign secretary condemned Iran's actions as "reckless threats" and the government agreed to allow US forces to use British bases, including Diego Garcia, for limited defensive operations targeting Iranian missile sites.
